articles.title: The Power He Chose Not to Use
articles.dek: Paul had every right to arrive in Corinth swinging. Instead, before he ever packed a bag, he told them exactly what he intended to do with his authority.
articles.quote: Authority is proven not by what it can tear down, but by what it chooses to build.
articles.body:
In March 1865, Abraham Lincoln climbed the steps of the Capitol to give his second inaugural address. The Civil War was ending, and everyone in that crowd knew it. Union armies had the Confederacy cornered. Powerful voices in the North were already calling for the hanging of Confederate leaders, a punishment severe enough to make sure no state ever tried this again. Lincoln commanded the largest army the continent had ever raised. He had every justification to make that speech about vengeance.

Instead he said something almost impossible for a man holding that much power to say: "With malice toward none, with charity for all... let us strive on to finish the work we are in... to bind up the nation's wounds." He was not weak. He simply decided, before the war was even fully won, what he would do with the power once it landed in his hands. He chose to build the nation back rather than tear the losing side apart.

Paul is standing at a smaller version of that same crossroads at the end of his second letter to Corinth. And the church has genuinely wounded him. Some members have questioned whether he is even a real apostle. Others have tolerated sin he had already confronted. He is coming a third time, and he has real authority to discipline, to expose, to make examples of people. The question is what he will do with it.

"This will be my third visit to you," he writes. "'Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses'" (13:1), quoting the old law that protected the accused from a single angry voice. Even walking into a fight, Paul insists on fairness. Then the warning sharpens: "I already gave you a warning when I was with you the second time. I now repeat it while absent: On my return I will not spare those who sinned earlier" (13:2). They had demanded proof that Christ actually speaks through him, so he answers with the strangest argument imaginable: "he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by God's power. Likewise, we are weak in him, yet by God's power we will live with him in our dealing with you" (13:4). His power, like his Lord's, would look like weakness right up until it didn't.

Then, before the confrontation even happens, Paul does something unusual. He turns the exam back on them. "Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves," he writes. "Do you not realize that Christ Jesus is in you—unless, indeed, you fail the test?" (13:5). He is not demanding they pass his inspection. He is inviting them to do their own honest accounting before he ever arrives, so that whatever happens next is theirs, not something done to them. "We are glad whenever we are weak but you are strong," he adds, "and our prayer is that you may be fully restored" (13:9). And then he says out loud, in ink, exactly what his authority is for.

"This is why I write these things when I am absent, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of authority—the authority the Lord gave me for building up, not for tearing down." (2 Corinthians 13:10, NIV)

Notice what he's doing. Most people decide how to use power in the heat of the moment, when the hurt is fresh and the other person is standing right in front of them. Paul decides in advance, in writing, while he's still hundreds of miles away and has every reason to be angry. He puts it on paper before the feelings of the actual confrontation can talk him out of it. That's exactly what Lincoln did on those Capitol steps: he named his intentions publicly before victory was complete, so that when the power was finally his to use, his own words would already be holding him to it.

It's worth asking what this means for the authority you actually carry. Maybe it's small compared to a president's or an apostle's — a parent over a child, a manager over an employee, an ate over a much younger kapatid, a barangay official over a complaint that landed on their desk. But everyone reading this holds some real power over someone, somewhere. And the test of that power is rarely decided in the moment it's used. It's decided earlier, quietly, in what you resolve to do with it before you're ever standing face to face with the person who hurt you.

Paul had grounds to arrive in Corinth and tear the place apart, and everyone would have understood why. He chose, ahead of time, to build instead. And when the hard letter finally ends, he doesn't close on the warning. He closes on this: "Finally, brothers and sisters, rejoice! Strive for full restoration, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace" (13:11), and then the words we now say over each other every Sunday without remembering where they came from: "May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all" (13:14). Even his very last sentence proves what he said in verse ten. He builds, right to the end.

So here's something worth keeping. Before your next hard conversation — with your child, your team, your kapatid, whoever it is you have some real say over — decide now, before you're in the room, what you intend to build. Write it down if you have to. Let your own words hold you to it later, the way Paul's did, the way Lincoln's did. The moment will tempt you to tear down. You get to decide today that you won't.

articles.title: The Ceremony That Forgot the Guest
articles.dek: A 16th-century tea master tore down Japan's most elaborate ritual to make room for something real — centuries after Isaiah had already named exactly what was missing.
articles.quote: God was never asking them to leave the temple. He was asking them to bring their hearts back into the room.
articles.illustration: Sen no Rikyu's tea ceremony reform
articles.body:
In the late 1500s, tea was the most powerful ritual in Japan. Warlords held tea gatherings the way modern executives hold state dinners: to display wealth, seal alliances, and remind everyone in the room exactly who held the power. The great feudal lord Oda Nobunaga collected rare tea bowls the way kings collected jewels, and owning the right one could be worth more than a castle. Guests arrived, performed the bows precisely, recited the right phrases of gratitude, admired the imported porcelain on cue. Every gesture was flawless. And almost none of it was about the person across the room.

Then a merchant's son named Sen no Rikyu became tea master to the two most powerful men in Japan, and he did something almost nobody expected. He shrank the tea room down to a hut the size of a walk-in closet, with a door so low that even a samurai had to remove his sword and bend at the waist just to crawl inside. He replaced gold and imported porcelain with plain clay bowls, some of them cracked and mended. He stripped away nearly everything that had made tea ceremonies impressive, because he had decided the ceremony was never supposed to be about the show. It was supposed to be two people, fully present with each other, for the length of one bowl of tea. He called it ichigo ichie: one time, one meeting, never to be repeated. The form only mattered if the heart was actually in the room.

Isaiah had already diagnosed the opposite problem, two thousand years earlier, in a much bigger room.

He's writing to Jerusalem, and he even calls the city "Ariel," a name that means something like altar hearth, because that's exactly what Jerusalem was: a city built around sacrifice, incense, feast days, and festivals (Isaiah 29:1). This isn't a godless city Isaiah is confronting. It's the most religiously busy city on earth. The calendar was full. The offerings kept coming. The choreography of worship never stopped. And God says: that's exactly the problem.

"The Lord says: 'These people come near to me with their mouth and honor me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me. Their worship of me is based on merely human rules they have been taught.'" (Isaiah 29:13)

Notice who God is describing. Not the cynics. Not the people who had walked away. The people still showing up, still singing the right words, still bringing the right offerings, still bowing at the right moment. Their mouths were near. Their hearts had quietly relocated somewhere else, and nobody, including them, had noticed the move.

That's the part worth sitting with. This isn't a passage about bad people faking devotion on purpose. It's a passage about good, busy, observant people whose worship had become so fluent that it no longer required their hearts to show up at all. You can say "I love you" the same way every night until the words stop needing your attention. You can pray the same grace over dinner until your mouth knows it by heart and your heart has left the table. The ritual doesn't break down when it goes hollow. That's exactly why it's so easy to miss. It keeps working perfectly on the outside.

Isaiah names the mechanism too: their worship "is based on merely human rules they have been taught" (Isaiah 29:13). Somewhere along the way, someone taught them the motions instead of the meeting. The words got passed down. The posture got passed down. But nobody can pass down the part where you actually meet God in the middle of it. That part is invisible. You can teach a child exactly when to bow and exactly what to say, but you cannot hand someone a heart that's paying attention. That, a person has to bring himself, every single time.

Isaiah adds one more line that explains why this drift is so dangerous: "the wisdom of the wise will perish, the intelligence of the intelligent will vanish" (Isaiah 29:14). The very people most skilled at the form are the ones least likely to notice their heart has gone missing, because skill is exactly what lets a person perform without thinking. The better you get at the choreography, the less it requires from you, and the less it requires from you, the easier it is to mistake fluency for presence.

This isn't only a temple problem. It's a marriage problem, a friendship problem, a family problem. "Kumusta ka" can be a real question or a hallway reflex. "I'm praying for you" can be a promise or a pleasant sign-off. A husband can kiss his wife goodbye every morning with his lips near and his mind three tasks ahead. Filipino warmth is famous for good reason: the mano po, the instinctive kain tayo, the smile that meets a stranger at the door. None of that has to be fake. But it's worth asking, every so often, whether the warmth is a doorway or a wall: a gesture that actually ushers someone into your attention, or a performance so practiced it no longer requires your attention at all.

Centuries after Isaiah, Jesus stood in front of religious leaders who knew their Bibles better than almost anyone alive, and he quoted this exact verse to them, word for word (Matthew 15:8-9). That's worth noticing too. God didn't retire this warning after Isaiah's generation. He handed it forward, because hearts drift the same way in every century, no matter how much scripture a person can quote.

Here's the good news hiding inside the warning: the fix was never "try harder at the ritual." Rikyu's guests didn't need better bows. They needed to actually be in the room with each other for the length of one bowl of tea. And what God asks for in Isaiah 29 isn't more sacrifices, more festivals, more perfectly executed liturgy. He never says improve your form. He says, in effect: come back. Bring the heart that already knows how to love, and simply point it at me again, in the same words you already know how to say.

So try this, maybe tonight. Pick one thing you say on repeat: grace before dinner, "I love you" at the door, a prayer you could recite half-asleep. Before you say it, take one breath. Let the words wait half a second for the heart to catch up to them. You don't need new words. You don't need a better ritual. You just need to actually be in the room when you say the ones you already have.

God was never asking them to leave the temple. He was asking them to bring their hearts back into the room.

articles.title: The Crag Was Built for Something Small
articles.dek: A tiny rock-dwelling creature in the Bible's own hills has an animal kingdom secret — and one verse in a creation psalm quietly explains why its safety looks nothing like the mountain goat's.
articles.quote: You don't have to be the wild goat to be safe on the mountain — sometimes God builds you a crag instead of a summit, and the crag is enough.
articles.body:
In the limestone cliffs above the Dead Sea, a small, ordinary-looking animal suns itself on a rock ledge that most tourists walk right past without a glance. It looks like an overgrown guinea pig — squat, brown, blunt-faced, about the size of a house cat. Zoologists call it a hyrax, though the King James Version of the Bible calls it a coney, and it has lived quietly on those same hillsides since long before anyone wrote a psalm about them. For centuries it was filed away as just another rodent, unremarkable. Then DNA testing changed everything. The hyrax's closest living relatives, it turns out, are not rabbits or rats. They are elephants and manatees. All three share a common ancestor from roughly sixty million years ago, and the hyrax still carries the family resemblance in miniature — tiny tusks, flattened toenails instead of claws, even a similar way of digesting tough plant fiber. It is, in effect, a distant cousin of the elephant that never got the memo about growing up.

But here is what makes the hyrax remarkable, not just curious. Unlike its giant relative, it has no size, no tusks worth fighting with, no speed to outrun a leopard or an eagle. It cannot dig a burrow the way a rabbit can. Its entire survival strategy is a rock. It has thick, rubbery pads on its feet, laced with sweat glands, that work almost like suction cups on sheer stone. When danger comes, the hyrax does not fight and does not outrun anything. It simply disappears into a crack in the mountain that was already there, waiting for something exactly its size.

It isn't a solitary creature either. Hyraxes live in colonies of dozens, and while most graze or doze in the sun, one is always posted on the highest visible rock, watching the sky. Let a shadow cross overhead and the sentry gives a sharp bark, and the whole colony vanishes into the crevices within seconds. They have turned smallness into a system: no single hyrax has to be strong, because the colony together builds what strength alone could never manage.

That is the picture the psalmist is painting in Psalm 104, a long, joyful hymn about God tending the whole of creation like a household. He waters the mountains from his upper chambers, and the land is satisfied by the fruit of his work, verse 13 says. He grows grass for the cattle and grain for people to farm, wine to gladden hearts, oil to make faces shine, bread to give strength, verses 14 and 15. He plants cedars in Lebanon so tall and well-watered that birds build nests in their branches and storks make their homes in the junipers, verses 16 and 17. It reads like a census of provision — every creature named, every need already met before it was ever felt.

Then the psalm reaches its final pair, and something quietly beautiful happens.

"The high mountains belong to the wild goats; the crags are a refuge for the hyrax." (Psalm 104:18, NIV)

Two animals, one verse, and they could not be more different. The wild goat is built for exposure — strong legs, perfect balance, born to stand on a ledge no wider than a hand, gazing out from the very top of the range. The hyrax never goes near the summit. It stays low, in the rock's hidden seams, out of sight, out of the wind.

Here is the detail worth sitting with: God did not give the hyrax a smaller, weaker version of the wild goat's gift. He did not simply scale down sure-footedness and hand the hyrax a lesser copy. He gave it something else entirely — a hiding place, custom-fit to what it actually is. The wild goat gets the mountain. The hyrax gets the crag. Neither is asked to become the other to be safe. The provision matches the creature, not some universal standard of strength.

It's worth noticing that the Bible circles back to this same small animal elsewhere, almost like it wants to make sure the point lands. Proverbs 30 lists four creatures that are small but remarkably wise, and one of them is this same rock-dweller: "hyraxes are creatures of little power, yet they make their home in the crags" (Proverbs 30:24, 26). Scripture does not treat the hyrax's smallness as a flaw to overcome. It treats the hiding place as wisdom — the right response to being small in a world full of things that are not.

Most of us know exactly which animal we feel like on any given week. Some days we are the wild goat — capable, visible, standing somewhere high and steady, and it feels good. But more days, if we are honest, we feel like the hyrax. Overlooked. Not the strongest voice in the room, not the one closing the big deal or leading the summit, but the one quietly arriving early to set up the chairs, or staying late to lock the gate after everyone else has gone home, just trying to find a place to be safe until tomorrow. There is a quiet shame that can creep in with that feeling, as if being small means being forgotten, as if safety was only ever built for the confident and the capable.

Psalm 104 says otherwise. The same God who planted cedars tall enough for storks measured the mountain down to its smallest crack, on purpose, for something that would never stand on the summit. The refuge was not an afterthought. It was written into the rock at creation, sized exactly for a creature that could never fight and would never need to, because the hiding place was already enough.

You do not have to become the wild goat to be safe on the mountain. You do not need more strength, more visibility, more sure-footed confidence than you actually have today. If today finds you low, hidden, and small — tired from work no one applauds, praying quietly for a family no one else is carrying, waiting in a season that has no view from the top — that is not evidence you have been missed. It may simply mean you have found the crag that was measured for you before you ever needed it. The crag is not a smaller mercy than the mountain. It is a mercy shaped precisely to fit you.

Carry this one line with you today: you don't have to be the wild goat to be safe on the mountain — sometimes God builds you a crag instead of a summit, and the crag is enough.

articles.title: The Heart No One Else Can Fully Read
articles.dek: A shoe return, a mother's death, and an old proverb about the loneliest true thing about being human — and the one who solves it.
articles.quote: Each heart knows its own bitterness, and no one else can share its joy.
articles.body:
In 2003, a woman called Zappos, the online shoe retailer, to return a pair of boots her mother had ordered but never got to wear. Her mother had died only days after the boots arrived. The woman just wanted to send them back — a small, practical task in the middle of a very large grief.

The customer service rep who answered didn't rush her off the phone with a return authorization number. She listened. She let the woman talk about her mother. When the call ended, the rep arranged the shipping label, refunded the order, and then, on her own initiative, sent flowers to the woman's home along with a card. No script told her to do that. No policy required it. She had simply noticed that underneath the return request was a heart carrying something the order form could never show.

Zappos built its whole customer service culture around moments like this. Reps are given wide freedom — no call-time limits, no scripts — because founder Tony Hsieh believed you cannot serve people well if you only process their words. You have to notice what's underneath them. It became one of the most retold customer-service stories in business schools, not because it was a clever marketing trick, but because it named something true: most of what people are carrying never shows up in what they say.

Three thousand years earlier, a different kind of wisdom teacher noticed the same thing. Proverbs 14 is one long, quick series of contrasts — the wise and the foolish, the mocker and the discerning, the reckless and the careful. Verse by verse it reads almost like a checklist: watch how you walk, watch who you walk with, watch what you say. And then, almost without warning, right in the middle of all that practical instruction, the writer turns inward and says something far more tender than anything around it.

Each heart knows its own bitterness, and no one else can share its joy. (Proverbs 14:10, NIV)

Read that twice. It's easy to skim past as a throwaway line about privacy. But sit with it and it becomes one of the most honest sentences in the whole book. Whatever bitterness you are carrying today — the diagnosis, the argument, the quiet disappointment nobody asked about — no one else can fully enter it. Not your spouse. Not your best friend. Not even the people who love you most. And whatever joy you are carrying — the answered prayer, the good news you haven't told anyone yet — no one else can fully share that either. It stays, at some level, yours alone.

It's worth asking why a book so full of practical advice about neighbors, cities, and kings would stop to say something this personal. Maybe because wisdom starts with an honest look at what people actually are: not fully knowable, even to each other. The rest of Proverbs 14 tells you how to walk carefully among people you cannot fully read — stay away from the fool whose heart you can't trust (v.7), give thought to your own ways since deception is easy (v.8), choose goodwill over mockery when someone needs to make things right (v.9). Verse 10 is the reason all that care is necessary. You are surrounded, every day, by hearts you cannot see into — and you are carrying one that no one else can fully see into either.

That could sound lonely. In one sense, it is. But it's also freeing, once you notice what it isn't saying. It isn't saying no one cares. It's saying no one — however loving — has the capacity to fully enter what only you carry. That takes an unfair weight off your relationships. Your husband isn't failing you because he can't feel your grief exactly as you feel it. Your friend isn't shallow because she can't share your joy at full strength. Proverbs 14:10 isn't an accusation. It's just telling the truth about being human, so you stop expecting people to do what people were never built to do.

And here is where the proverb quietly points past itself. Scripture doesn't leave no one else can share it as the last word on the human heart. Isaiah calls the coming Messiah "a man of suffering, and familiar with pain" (Isaiah 53:3) — someone who didn't just hear about bitterness but entered it. Hebrews says Jesus endured the cross "for the joy set before him" (Hebrews 12:2) — someone who didn't just admire joy from a distance but ran toward it through suffering. The one relationship Proverbs 14:10 doesn't quite anticipate is a Savior who became fully human so that, for the first time, a heart's bitterness and a heart's joy could actually be shared — not just observed, but carried. What no other person can do for you, Christ can. "You have searched me, Lord, and you know me" (Psalm 139:1). That's not poetry about surveillance. That's the answer to Proverbs 14:10.

So what do you do with a heart no one else can fully read? Two small things. First, stop waiting for a person to do what only God can do. Take the bitterness you're carrying straight to him today — not the polished version, the real one — because he is the one being in the universe who actually can share it. Second, don't let "no one can fully know" become an excuse to stop trying. The Zappos rep couldn't fully enter a stranger's grief either. She sent flowers anyway. You won't ever fully know what's underneath your coworker's short temper or your neighbor's silence. Reach toward them anyway, with one small, undeserved kindness — what verse 9 calls goodwill. You may not solve their bitterness. You might still be the moment someone remembers as the day their heart felt a little less alone.

Today, try this: name the one thing in your heart that no one else fully carries — and say it out loud to God, plainly, the way you would to someone who could actually hold it. Because you have one. And then look for a single person today whose heart you can't read either, and do for them what that rep did with a shoebox and a florist's card: something small, undeserved, and kind. You won't share their whole heart. But you might just lighten it.
